newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FAA chief Hinson announces his resignation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FAA chief Hinson announces his resignation.

text.p: Federal Aviation Administrator David Hinson announced Thursday he had submitted his resignation to President Clinton and will step down from his job on Saturday.
The FAA said his deputy, Linda Hall Daschle, will serve as acting administrator through January 31.
A successor to Hinson, 63, has not been announced.

"I promised the president I would serve through his first term," he said in a statement, "and with his help, and that of Secretary Pena and Linda Daschle, we have made exceptional progress in giving the FAA a new focus and direction."
Federico Pena is secretary of the Transportation Department, the FAA's parent agency. Daschle is the wife of Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle, a South Dakota Democrat.
Hinson, who served as FAA chief for nearly three years, added in his statement that he was proud to have served the president and to have contributed to making flying safer.
Pena, who is reported also to be resigning, said in statement that "David Hinson's outstansding leadership fundamentally transformed the FAA over the past three years."
Hinson has said he counts among his accomplishments as FAA administrator an internal reform of the agency, including speeding up the modernisation of the nation's ageing air traffic control system.

Congress, pressed by the agency, passed legislation to allow the FAA to write its own personnel and procurement rules so it could respond more quickly to the nation's increased air traffic and to buy the new technology to cope with it.
In addition, Hinson oversaw the tightening of safety regulations for small commuter aircraft to bring them up to the safety standards of the big jet airliners.

He also has been back of an effort to have airlines exchange with other airlines their data on aircraft anomolies so an incident one carrier discovers on it plane is not a system-wide design flaw which could make the plane accident prone.
It was under Hinson's administration that the agency stepped up its inspection of new, start-up airlines to assure they closely followed all airworthiness regulations.
That move was taken after the May crash of ValuJet flight 592 near Miami, killing all 110 people on board.
Low-fare ValuJet was grounded five weeks later, cited for widespread violations of repair and maintenace regulations.
The carrier has since resumed flying.
Before taking over the FAA, Hinson had been a navy and commercial airline pilot and airline and aerospace executive.
